interactions.summary: Jiang glosses the canto as identity theft and asks why Dante unusually dwells on metamorphosis in exhaustive detail rather than moving on quickly.

Students speculate that the long metamorphosis description may contrast hell's microscopic restriction with heaven's expansiveness, dramatize dehumanization, or let Dante compete openly with Ovid on metamorphosis.

claims.claim: Jiang identifies these sinners as impostors or identity thieves whose punishment fits the crime because their bodies and souls are repeatedly overtaken, dispersed, and remade.
Jiang treats the canto's unusual descriptive length as a real interpretive problem, noting that Dante is usually terse and economical rather than exhaustive.
A student proposes that the microscope-like attention to metamorphosis makes hell feel like the inverse of heaven's expansiveness and grandeur.
Another student argues that lingering over metamorphosis underscores the sinners' progressive loss of humanity.
A third student suggests Dante is also staging a poetic contest with Ovid by showing that he can write metamorphosis scenes just as powerfully.

signature_moments.moment: Identity theft becomes literalized as bodies that can no longer hold a stable self.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Snakes take over their bodies and then dissipates their soul
signature_moments.why_it_matters: Jiang turns a modern fraud analogy into a metaphysical image of social trust and personhood coming apart.

signature_moments.moment: The class imagines Dante writing this canto partly to prove he can do metamorphosis as well as Ovid.
signature_moments.source_phrase: prove that he can write about metamorphosis as good as Ovid can
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It reframes the canto as literary rivalry as well as moral punishment.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's modern analog for this bolgia: imposture and fraud so deep that the sinner's very body becomes unstable.
